cards/1/q: Implement Queue using Stacks (#232): Push goes onto stack in; Pop takes from stack out, and if out is empty, it first moves all of in into it. What does Pop cost?
cards/1/options/0: O(1) amortized: each element moves from in to out at most once
cards/1/options/1: O(n) always: every Pop moves the whole stack
cards/1/options/2: O(log n): the transfer splits the stack in half
cards/1/explain: The transfer reverses the order: the top of out is the oldest element, just as a queue needs. An expensive Pop happens only when out is empty, and it pays for elements each of which travels in → out exactly once in its lifetime. The same argument as for the monotonic stack: at most 2n operations for n elements.
cards/1/wrong/1: The transfer happens only when out is empty. After it, the following Pops take from out in O(1) until it runs dry.
cards/1/wrong/2: The whole of in is moved at once; nothing is split in half. The cost is O(1) on average per element.
cards/2/q: Online Stock Span (#901): next(price) for each new day returns how many consecutive days, including today, the price was not above today’s. What do you keep on the stack so that next costs O(1) amortized?
cards/2/options/0: (price, span) pairs: a new price pops every pair with a price not above its own and adds up their spans
cards/2/options/1: All prices ever seen: the span is computed by scanning back
cards/2/options/2: Only the highest price ever seen
cards/2/explain: This is “the nearest greater to the left”: the span is the distance to the last day with a higher price. Popped pairs are no longer needed: the new price is not below them, and any future day that covers it will cover them too — so their spans fold into its span. Each pair enters and leaves once.
cards/2/wrong/1: Scanning back is O(n) per call, and O(n²) in total on rising prices. The monotonic stack removes exactly that repeated work.
cards/2/wrong/2: The maximum does not tell you where the run ends: on prices 100, 60, 70 the answer for 70 is 2, and the maximum 100 does not show that.
cards/3/task: Step through Largest Rectangle in Histogram on [4, 2, 3, 3, 1]. The rig stops twice: on equal heights and on the last bar.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: push 3: no need to pop an equal bar
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: i = 3, height 3. The stack holds indices 1 (height 2) and 2 (height 3), with 2 on top. The heights are equal. What does the code do?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: The >= condition pops an equal bar too. Below it is index 1, so left = 2, width 3 − 2 = 1, area 3 — undercounted. That is not a bug: the height-3 rectangle over indices 2–3 will be counted in full by index 3 when it is popped.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: i = 4, height 1. Index 3 has been popped: width 2, area 6. Only index 1 of height 2 is left in the stack. What does the code count?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: 2 ≥ 1 — pop it. The stack is empty, so left = 0: there is no bar lower than 2 to the left — the four was popped back on the first step. Width 4 − 0 = 4, area 8 — a record and the answer.
cards/4/q: On [70, 70, 75] this code returns [1, 1, 0] instead of [2, 1, 0]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: The day must be strictly warmer, but <= also pops a day with the same temperature: at i = 1 the second 70° day “closes” the first one, and ans[0] = 1. It must be t[stack.Peek()] < t[i] — then equal days wait together, and 75° closes both.
cards/5/q: Next Greater Element II (#503): a circular array; for each element, the nearest greater value, or −1.
cards/5/explain: The second lap goes over the same elements, hence nums[i % n]. The answer here is a value, not a distance, so ans = x. Push only the indices of the first lap: the second lap exists only so that elements near the end can see the start of the array.
cards/6/q: Palindrome Linked List (#234) with O(1) memory: find the middle with fast and slow pointers, reverse the second half, compare the halves. What does it cost, and what is worth telling the interviewer?
cards/6/options/0: O(n) time, O(1) memory; after the check, reverse the second half back — the caller does not expect the list to change
cards/6/options/1: O(n log n): reversing half the list is a sort
cards/6/options/2: O(n) time and O(n) memory for a reversed copy
cards/6/explain: The middle takes n/2 steps, reversing the half n/2, comparing n/2: O(n). The reversal is in place, with three pointers — O(1) memory. But it modifies the input list, which may be referenced from outside: a careful solution restores the half with the same reversal.
cards/6/wrong/1: A reversal compares nothing and orders nothing: it is one pass with three pointers.
cards/6/wrong/2: No copy is needed: the second half is reversed in place by rewiring links.
cards/7/q: Game code and .NET. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: A UI screen stack: Back is Pop and show the new top
cards/7/options/1: Recursively reversing a list of 10⁶ nodes in Unity is safe: IL2CPP turns the recursion into a loop
cards/7/options/2: An index-based list struct Node { int value; int next; } can be walked in a Burst job
cards/7/options/3: LinkedList<T>.AddLast(value) in every Update creates garbage
cards/7/options/4: A Min Stack on pairs loses the minimum after push 3, push 3, pop
cards/7/explain: The screen below the top is the previous one, and that is what we show. Neither C# nor IL2CPP promises to turn recursion into a loop, and this reversal is not even a tail call — 10⁶ frames overflow the stack. An array of structs without references is unmanaged; NativeArray and Burst accept it. AddLast(value) is a new heap node on every call. Each three carries its own minimum in its pair: after the pop the top is (3, 3).
cards/8/q: You are solving Min Stack out loud at an interview. Put the steps in order.
cards/8/items/0: Clarify: all four operations in O(1), the value range, no calls on an empty stack
cards/8/items/1: Naive: GetMin by scanning — O(n); a single min field breaks when Pop removes the minimum
cards/8/items/2: Idea: the minimum depends only on what lies below an element — store it next to the element on insertion
cards/8/items/3: Code: Stack<(int val, int min)>, Push takes Math.Min(val, Peek().min)
cards/8/items/4: Run push 2, push 2, pop: the minimum stays 2
cards/8/items/5: Complexity: O(1) per operation, 2n numbers of memory
cards/8/items/6: The two-stack variant and why it needs x <= mins.Peek()
cards/8/explain: The problem, the baseline and where it breaks, the idea and the code, a run on duplicates — the trickiest case, the complexity, and finally the variant you will be asked about next.
